Have had PTSD since childhood do to parental neglect, along with physical (and yes sexual) and mental abuse. I've been in treatment for years, but occasionally develop states of psychosis and suffer various hallucinations (voices, audio, visual) and paranoia. Currently on a regime of antipsychotics, and am now in outpatient care. Go ahead and ask me anything.
I am a sufferer of severe PTSD currently working through a period of psychosis, AMA.

Pretty good. I took my evening tranquilizer, and so far it is just a good night with my kids and listening to an audiobook about economics. Earlier was just a bit unsettling, had a lot of 'background' noise in my head as I kept hearing voices whispering around me that I couldn't make out, but that has passed now.
What can we do, to help you? (I mean this from the point of view that we have no idea what you're going through.)

Well, if we were to meet, I'd say the best way to make my life easier is to always try and be direct in your communication. A lot of times people don't realize how much of a social deficit being mentally ill can create in a person, how social cues and such will go right over my head most days. So when people rely less on being indirect, or 'polite', etc, it actually makes it a lot easier to engage with me and not cause needless friction, especially when I am not having the best grip of reality.

There has been a few occasions where I came across someone who asked me something, in a highly adgetated state, emotionally worked up. I chose to listen to their words and answered the question based only on the words. Things went well, when I did not react to their emotional state. I do this all the time now.
How often do you go to hospitals or other facilities for treatment? How long is an average stay? How were you first diagnosed?

About once a month, mostly for blood test because of the medicines I am on. But I check in with my psychiatrist once every two weeks, and usually see the psychologist once a week in person and phone session as needed.

Average stay is kind of hard to say, as there is no average incident or problem. Also it depends what type of insurance I have at the time. But I'd say most are seventy two hours, and usually mostly about determining I am not suicidal or a danger to anyone.

When I was in the army, I took a psychological evaluation after I suffered a concussion and my primary doctor saw the symptoms of a psychotic state then.

If you are open to discussing them, what were the symptoms your primary doctor saw?

Based on your username and your other responses, you might be autistic. Do you think you are? If so, how has being diagnosed with PTSD changed your autism?

I really hope this AMA had a positive effect on you.

The biggest was a demeanor of detachment from the emotional consequences of my injuries, but more so from the events of my life. When we'd talk about the possibility of brain damage, or lingering effects of the other injuries I sustained, the doctor noted I seemed unable to discuss things in a way that showed I could see things getting better. I had an aura of fatalism about me, but without the melancholy of someone in a depression I would say was the best way to describe what he picked up on. That and the overly defensive reactions I could have at times.

As for autism, I mean I do not think I am an autistic. Then again I also do not think such a thing as a 'high functioning autistic' even exist. That said, I would say that given my family history with autism (the type some would call low functioning), I would say that yes as a spectrum I touch on certain points of it to a degree. As far as diagnosis, most of the mental health professionals I've seen stay away from it. Given the pronounced symptoms of severe PTSD, they do not see, nor do I, much benefit to my treatment to pursue a diagnosis like that when I have more severe quality of life impacting issues to tackle.

I think it will, as it is good to put it down in words, and re-read my answers. Makes it easier to reason through exactly where I am in handling my illness.
What does it feel like? When you start to hallucinate or hear voices. Does the world around you kind of grey out? Edit: Thanks for doing this. Its pretty interesting.

Happy to, and the single best way to describe when I start to experience a hallucination is confusion. Sometimes it comes with dread, or even outright terror. But more so it is confusion. Is what I am seeing, hearing, feeling, believing, real? Why is my mind telling me one thing, but my senses another? Which is right? A good analogy for it is a stranger walks up to you, and starts talking to you directly on the most intimate details of your life that you barely ever even reflect or admit to yourself. That's what the audio hallucinations are like. Sometimes I can tell it is just a runaway internal dialogue in my mind, and work it out, but a lot of other times not. As for the visual stuff, it is usually things in the dark taking shape and coming at me. Usually in the form of dark shapes coming to attack me or my family. Or imagining I am hearing something trying to get in my house and get me as I try to relax, or fall asleep. Having a dog, and focusing on the fact that the odds of someone sneaking up on the house without the dog knowing is a great help to help me calm myself.

Thanks for doing this again. I'm truly sorry this happened to you and good on you for dealing with it like you are. Props to your family too I imagine it can get hard on all of you. I don't mean to sound like a dick or anything, but it is amazing how the human brain deals with stress and trauma in different manners.
How different are you during "good" and "bad" episodes?

Drastically, depending on how far I am from properly and realistically assessing things. Add to that military training, and it can get rather bad as the 'don't stop, dead people stop' thinking kicks in that puts you into an aggressive posture always looking to take initiative which is a really bad thing when you just are in no place to determine what is a rational action. Needless to say, I am terrified of interactions with law enforcement. Police are just not trained to deal with the severely mentally ill, but they are trained to react to aggressive behavior very forcefully as the best defense for their own lives.

Honestly though, the real 'bad' from me is the emotional consequences of when I lose touch with reality. Like when I was misreading the stress my wife was under from a multitude of things, let alone my illness, and began to believe and treat her as if she were having an affair. She wasn't, but I literally talked myself into believing she was. In retrospect, I'm still rattled, have guilt, and am angry at myself for that episode. To turn on my biggest advocate like that, to believe without doubt the person I love most was doing that to me with no rational evidence or reasonable suspicion is very hard to come to grips with.

Its way beyond looking for attention, and into some serious issues of lacking self confidence, or as Kaczynski put it, never experiencing the power process.
